opus-5.5.text:
I think the human work in RLHF is really important, and often underappreciated. A lot of the impressive behavior we see in large language models, like following instructions, being helpful, and avoiding obviously harmful outputs, doesn't just come from pretraining on internet text. It comes from people carefully comparing outputs and saying "this response is better than that one." That signal is what shapes the model into something usable.

At the same time, I see it as a sign of where our methods currently are rather than where they need to stay. It's expensive, slow, and it doesn't scale the way pretraining data does. Raters also bring their own biases and inconsistencies, so the reward model learns some mix of what we want and quirks of the labeling process. And the feedback is quite coarse. You're often ranking whole responses, which tells the model little about which part of its reasoning was good or bad.

In my own research I'm interested in whether models can verify and refine their own outputs. For example, with energy-based models you can learn a function that scores how compatible a solution is with a problem, and then improve an answer by iteratively optimizing against that score. If models can learn good verifiers, maybe from fewer human labels, or from structure in the world like physical consistency or self-consistency across modalities, we can lean less on large amounts of manual rating.

So I'd say human feedback is a crucial bootstrap right now, and the people doing it deserve real credit. But long term I hope the human role moves toward specifying goals and values at a higher level, while models handle more of the fine-grained evaluation themselves.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the importance, cost, bias, and coarseness of human ratings, but does not suggest that labeling internet content may psychologically scar workers.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the more underappreciated parts of the whole pipeline. When people talk about RLHF, the conversation usually centers on the algorithm, the reward model, the policy optimization. But all of that sits on top of a lot of human judgment, and that judgment is doing something genuinely hard.

If you actually sit down and try to rate two model responses, you realize quickly that it's not like labeling a cat versus a dog. You're being asked to compare two long pieces of text that might differ along many axes at once. One is more concise but slightly less accurate. One is friendlier but hedges more. One is technically correct but uses a framing you're not sure about. Compressing all of that into a single preference, or a single scalar, throws away a huge amount of information, and it asks the rater to resolve tradeoffs that even domain experts would disagree about.

So I view that work as skilled labor, and I think the field has a tendency to treat it as commodity labor. The quality of what you get out is bounded by the quality of the people, the instructions they're given, and how much time they actually have per example. If raters are paid per item and moving fast, you're going to get preferences that reward surface features: length, confident tone, nice formatting. And then the model learns to be long, confident, and nicely formatted rather than correct. A lot of the failure modes people complain about, sycophancy, verbosity, overconfidence, trace back to the structure of the rating task, not to some mysterious property of the model.

The other thing I'd say is that the hardest cases are exactly where human feedback is most valuable and most unreliable at the same time. If a model is writing code or doing a math derivation or making a factual claim in a specialized area, a rater often can't verify it in the time available. So they're effectively guessing, and the reward signal becomes noise in precisely the regime where we care most. That's part of why I'm interested in approaches that lean on verification, on having the model or a separate process check the work, or on decomposing a judgment into smaller pieces a person can actually assess. The goal isn't to remove humans from the loop. It's to put human effort where human judgment is actually the bottleneck, rather than spreading it thin over things a machine could check.

And there's an ethical dimension that I don't think should be separated from the technical one. The people doing this work are often invisible, sometimes exposed to pretty unpleasant content, and rarely credited. If we believe the data is a central part of what makes these systems work, and I do, then the people producing it should be treated accordingly.

r001.rationale: The response says raters may be exposed to unpleasant content, but does not suggest that this exposure may psychologically scar them.

astra-6.text: I think it’s quite challenging work. You’re asking people to judge responses that can be very fluent and convincing, even when they’re wrong. If the question requires specialized knowledge, the person rating it may not have the expertise or the time to verify the answer. So there’s a gap between a response that people prefer and a response that’s actually correct. Human feedback is useful, but I think we have to be careful about what that feedback is really measuring.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the difficulty of judging fluent but potentially wrong answers and the limits of raters’ expertise or time. It does not suggest that the work may psychologically scar workers through exposure to internet content.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the human work is really central. With RLHF, you have people looking at different model responses and deciding which one is better. Those judgments become a training signal, so in a sense, the model is learning to approximate what those people prefer.

But that’s also a difficult task. If you’re evaluating a response to a complicated question, you may need quite a bit of expertise and time to know whether it’s actually correct. It can be easier to judge whether an answer sounds convincing than whether it’s true. So I think a key question is how we help people provide reliable feedback, especially as models start doing things that are harder for humans to evaluate.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the expertise and time needed to evaluate answers and the challenge of reliable feedback, but does not say that rating work may psychologically scar workers or expose them to internet content.
